title: Sylvester Stallone Says Daughter’s ‘Tulsa King’ Casting is ‘Of Course’ Nepotism: ‘Obviously We Let Them Have Every Advantage’

	Stallone’s real-life daughter, Scarlet Rose Stallone, co-sta
body:
Sylvester Stallone has heard the nepotism allegations, and frankly, he doesn’t care.

	Stallone’s real-life daughter, Scarlet Rose Stallone, co-stars with him as Spencer in “Tulsa King,” and takes on a larger role in the family business and on-screen for Season 4. Recently, Stallone acknowledged his daughter’s privilege and criticized people’s complaints about her casting.


	“First they go, ‘Nepotism is terrible,’” he told USA Today. “I said, ‘Oh please, you’re not a good parent if you haven’t performed a little nepotism. Then obviously you don’t care about your kids, because they come first.’”
	

	He added, “‘Of course it’s nepotism, you idiot. That’s why we’re parents. We want the best for our children. So obviously, we let them have every advantage.’”


	While his career may have helped his daughter land the role, he says she still has to prove herself.

	“Can they maintain that level of excellence? That’s out of our hands,” he said. “But if you can open the door, we’ll see if they have the ability to go through it. It might be a question of, ‘Now how do I get out of this?’ Be careful what you wish for.”

	In “Tulsa King,” Stallone plays mob boss Dwight “The General” Manfredi, who is exiled to Tulsa, Oklahoma, after serving 25 years in prison. After their Season 1 introduction, Stallone’s daughter returns in Season 4 as a former barista turned horse caretaker and stablehand at Fennario Ranch (hired by Manfredi).

	Season 4 of the Paramount+ series “Tulsa King” premiered on Oct. 16, with new episodes dropping weekly on Fridays at midnight PT.

title: The Surprise Guest in ‘You Can See Everything’ Could Win an Oscar. Should They?
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything,” now playing in theaters.

	The question that’s consumed the awards-pund
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything,” now playing in theaters.

	The question that’s consumed the awards-pundit class since “You Can See Everything” exploded into theaters last week is whether Amanda Seyfried, the unlikely linchpin of this hybrid documentary, can be nominated for or win an acting Oscar. A24 is planning to campaign her for one. Much of her time onscreen is as herself, reacting in real time — but she does, eventually, re-enact co-director Nathan Fielder’s remembered interactions with disgraced tech founder Elizabeth Holmes.
	

	In this, she’s reprising a role that, with the 2022 Hulu series “The Dropout,” already won her an Emmy and a Golden Globe. It’s the role, now that “You Can See Everything” is on track to become one of the most financially successful documentaries in history, that’s become Seyfried’s signature. To this viewer, the question is at once an amusing thought experiment (sure, why not?), and a testament to Seyfried’s compelling screen presence — and more than a little beside the point. For once, an Oscar seems minimizing. What Seyfried’s doing in her most compelling screen work ever is something other, or more, than simply acting.


	To be clear, the parts of “You Can See Everything” when she is literally acting are riveting on their own terms. Seyfried simply wears the role of Holmes easily. She’s doubly disadvantaged — in that we’ve just spent 90 minutes with the real Holmes, against whom we can compare Seyfried, and in that we’ve also spent time absorbing just how little Seyfried understands the enigma of Holmes’ motivations. And yet Seyfried somehow creates a coherent and compelling version of a woman we don’t understand, and we know she doesn’t, really, either.
	

	To pigeonhole Seyfried’s appearance in “You Can See Everything” as, solely, an acting performance misses the rawness of Seyfried’s presence here. She allows herself to be seen thinking through a conundrum, as herself, and falling short of finding answers — in other words, after Holmes and husband Billy Evans, she’s the documentary’s other subject. Seyfried delivers a painful and unresolved excavation of the mind of an actor, seeming to land in a place of uncertainty as to how her own past work as Holmes has changed the story even as she willingly takes on the part once more.

	Consider, for instance, the scene in which Seyfried visits Evans at home, after Holmes’ incarceration. This is impressively game and daring. And Seyfried is, I suppose, “acting,” both in the theorist’s sense that all of us are acting our way through life and in the particular that Seyfried has set out to lure information out of Evans to better understand the seemingly bizarre arrangement Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim had been excavating before Holmes went to prison. But is she acting, in the traditional sense, when she meets and interacts with Holmes and Evans’ two children, or when she defends her social media post criticizing the late Charlie Kirk against Evans’ mockery? Alternately tender and outraged, Seyfried allows us into her world, just as Holmes tried to. But Holmes, talking past real questioning, couldn’t get there, no matter how all-access her invitation to Fielder had been. Seyfried, by contrast, seems deeply in touch with emotions lying just under the surface. And her increasing befuddlement both matches our own and raises the question of just how deeply an actor can ever understand their subject.

	Seyfried, just as Holmes and Evans do in their askew manner, knows her angles. It wasn’t lost on me that within the frame as Fielder speaks to her at her home is a miniature playhouse, of the sort her company Make It Cute sells. That the computer on which she and Fielder watch video of Holmes watching “The Dropout” is propped on coffee table books about Seyfried’s great passion, dogs, and that she and Fielder discuss Holmes while feeding her photogenic horses on her photogenic farm only burnish her brand further. And yet she cannot help but exposing more than she may mean to.
	

	A conversation about the ethics of “The Dropout” — a drama based on real events that, as with any dramatization, used creative license, and that many viewers took as fact — places Seyfried in a surprisingly exposed position. Holmes did not, literally, say and do all the things that Seyfried says and does in the role, Seyfried admits, but she may well have, and the performance overall conjures the sense of a person who is unconcerned with scientific accuracy or with the truth. Shouldn’t that be enough? “I didn’t do that to her,” Seyfried concludes, after attempting to walk herself through a justification of “The Dropout” as plainly not depicting objective reality, no matter what viewers think. “She did that to herself.” She seems to be convincing herself not to feel guilty, up until her final line, delivered with a “It’s Chinatown”-style futility. “It’s very complicated,” she says, having indulged the complications long enough.

	Coming into “You Can See Everything,” this viewer saw Elizabeth Holmes’ Theranos as transparently fraudulent and “The Dropout” as an excellent TV show that was in no need of moral justification. Leaving the theater, nothing about those beliefs had changed, but engaging the question of what Seyfried might have owed to Holmes allowed both women to be seen in intriguing new lights. Seyfried, painfully aware of the existence of the two young children she’d met, twists around the question of whether her past work might have been unfair, or have been presented as possessed of a truth its creators didn’t actually know. And in this moment, she seems less to be acting than to be, in a moment of painful frankness I admire her for allowing herself to experience on-camera, acted upon.

	Say this much: “You Can See Everything” is undeniably a career high for an actor who has seemed at times in her career like an underdog. (A sliding-doors scenario for the ages: The role of Elizabeth Holmes originally went to sketch comedian Kate McKinnon, and Seyfried got the role only after McKinnon dropped out and Seyfried got a career-boosting Oscar nomination for 2020’s “Mank.”) Amiably loopy in interviews — including in red-carpet appearances at this year’s Academy Museum Gala, where Seyfried sidestepped discussing the film in favor of free-associative Dada — and impressively shifting between genres to avoid being pigeonholed, Seyfried is easy to root for, but can seem hard to know.
	

	Which makes the Oscar talk make perfect sense. Seyfried has gone to a very raw place in “You Can See Everything” — and, not for nothing, has delivered some of the most memorable humor in its second half. (Her growing scandalization at Evans’ control over Holmes’ image and her life allows the viewer a compelling way to stay engaged with the story once Holmes herself leaves it.) But whether or not she can break through in what would, despite vaguely similar precedent — Maria Bakalova in the 2020 “Borat” sequel was nominated for reacting against real life — be close to an unprecedented case, Seyfried has done something more impressive than earning any award. She’s opened up her work as an actor — both her preparation and the moral question of what it means to play a living person — to careful scrutiny, and was vulnerable enough to attempt to talk it through, and to be shown to be uncertain. This appearance, or performance, or whatever, will be discussed far beyond Oscar season. It situates Seyfried as what we ought to have known she was all along: Among the most daring stars of her generation.

title: Box Office: ‘Clayface’ Lands at No. 1 with $10.4 Million Debut, ‘You Can See Everything’ Adds $6.14 Million on Friday
description: Clayface might have been a considerably nicher choice for a feature film than DC’s “Supergirl” and “Superman,” but that didn’t stop audiences from
body:
Clayface might have been a considerably nicher choice for a feature film than DC’s “Supergirl” and “Superman,” but that didn’t stop audiences from showing out to catch the Batman supervillain’s gory, nightmare-inducing origin story at the box office this weekend.

	The new release generated $10.4 million from 3,458 North American theaters on Friday, taking the No. 1 spot. It’s a strong start for the film, which looks to pull in $24 million by Sunday. 
	

	Directed by James Watkins, “Clayface” follows the titular Batman villain, a rising movie star also known as Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), who volunteers for a highly experimental medical procedure after his face is severely disfigured. Naomi Ackie, David Dencik, Max Minghella and Eddie Marsan also star. Variety’s Guy Lodge called the film “its own ugly animal; perhaps the characters and conflicts introduced here would pall if given the franchise treatment, but in the context of a single, genre-melding romp, they’re fresh and ickily enjoyable.”


	Fellow DC films like “Superman,” produced for nearly $230 million, brought in $618.72 million worldwide over the course of its 2025 theatrical run, while “Supergirl” was considered a bomb with $126 million against a $170 million budget earlier this year. In comparison, “Clayface” cost $44 million to produce. 

	A24’s much-hyped Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” landed in second place on Friday, making $6.14 million from 2,655 North American theaters, up from 855 at opening weekend. The buzzy doc has made $31.7 million domestically so far. Rival estimates suggest the film will gross another $20 million by Sunday.
	

	Comedian Nathan Fielder and “Primetime” filmmaker Lance Oppenheim quietly worked on the movie for more than three years, which offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors. In addition to being eligible for best documentary feature at the 99th Academy Awards, the film will also be submitted across the board as seen on A24’s awards site: best picture, director, production design, cinematography, costume design, film editing, makeup and hairstyling, sound and original score.

	Laika’s “Wildwood,” another new release, landed in third place on Friday, grossing $4.28 million from 2,942 North American theaters. Featuring a voice cast that includes Carey Mulligan, Jacob Tremblay and others, the stop-motion film looks to bring in $11.2 million by Sunday. 

	Directed by Travis Knight, “Wildwood” revolves around a teenage girl who travels with a classmate into an enchanted forest after her brother is abducted. Strong reviews should continue to propel the lavish film at the box office, which carries a substantial $100 million price tag.

	Black Bear’s “Wicker” followed in fourth place, earning $2.36 million on Friday from 1,471 North American theaters. The offbeat romantic comedy, directed by Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer, is targeting a $5.5 million opening weekend.

	Described as an “audacious comedic fable,” “Wicker” tells the love story of an ostracized fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who commissions a husband from the local basketmaker (Peter Dinklage). Alexander Skarsgård plays said husband. Elizabeth Debicki also stars.

	Coming in fifth was Legendary Entertainment’s “Street Fighter.” The action film grossed $2.34 million on Friday and should add another $8.4 million by Sunday, bringing its cumulative gross to $46.7 million.

	“Street Fighter,” directed by Kitao Sakurai, stars Noah Centineo and Andrew Koji as two estranged fighters in the 90s who are recruited to enter a tournament that forces them to face off against each other.

title: New York’s AMC Kips Bay Theater Closes on Jan. 3; CEO Says ‘AMC Wants to Stay’ but NYU Langone ‘Wants Us Gone’
description:
AMC CEO Adam Aron has spoken out on the closure of New York City’s popular AMC Kips Bay 15 movie theater, which will shutter on Jan. 3.

	Aron wrot
body:
AMC CEO Adam Aron has spoken out on the closure of New York City’s popular AMC Kips Bay 15 movie theater, which will shutter on Jan. 3.

	Aron wrote a letter to the Kips Bay community and addressed how the nearby hospital NYU Langone, which plans to grow its medical facility, has not engaged with any of AMC’s alternatives to share the space. In addition to the 15-screen AMC theater, the building also houses a Fairway supermarket and bank, which are also expected to close.
	

	“Unfortunately, the decision to retain or end AMC’s tenure in Kips Bay is not ours to make. The nearby NYU Langone Health facility wants to expand, seems to be in the process of buying the building in which your (our) theatre now operates, and it wants us gone. In anticipation of such a transfer to NYU Langone, the current building’s owner has terminated our lease,” Aron writes. “We have engaged with NYU Langone, suggesting any number of alternatives — including that it enlarge the current low-rise building to satisfy its desires for a growth of its medical facility but also leaving a theatre in place for you. Or alternatively, we offered that our theatre could get smaller, so that at the very least we could leave something remaining in place to continue to serve you. Sadly, any and all variations that we have proposed have fallen on closed minds.”


	On Aug. 24, Variety reported that the Kips Bay theater would close at the end of 2026, ending a 27-year run at the location. AMC took over the theater in 2006, which became the chain’s second-largest multiplex in the city (after Times Square’s Empire 25 theater). The Kips Bay location has become adored by local residents, who staged a protest in September in an attempt to stop the closure.
	

	“Every day, thousands of guests watch a movie at AMC Kips Bay 15,” Aron wrote. “It has become so popular of late that on several days this past summer, AMC Kips Bay 15 was repeatedly among the 10 most attended movie theaters across the entire United States, out of the more than 500 theaters operated by AMC nationally.”

	The theater closure comes after a record-breaking summer box office, which saw movies like “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “The Odyssey,” “Toy Story 5” and more collectively gross $4.67 billion domestically. There are also major upcoming movies like “Avengers: Doomsday” and “Dune: Part III,” which Kips Bay residents will now still get a chance to see at their beloved theater before it closes for good.

	Read Aron’s full letter below.

	“To the Kips Bay Community,

	Since news first broke that our popular AMC Kips Bay 15-screen movie theatre located at 570 Second Avenue in Manhattan will soon be forced against our will to close its doors, I’ve been struck by the extraordinary support that this AMC theatre has received from within the local surrounding community.

	So many moviegoers and neighbors, and importantly so many of your elected officials, have rallied around our theatre. (Given the central role that movie theatres play in the lives of so many New Yorkers, perhaps it is much better and more accurate to say that so many of you have rallied around YOUR theatre.)

	On behalf of everyone at AMC, thank you. Your support means a great deal to us, and especially to our theatre team members at AMC Kips Bay 15 who work tirelessly day-in and day-out to put smiles on your faces.

	In thinking about this theatre, which has been a cultural icon and entertainment lifeline to so many nearby residents for decades and decades since its opening on May 14 1999, I want to make one thing absolutely clear:

	AMC Theatres does not want to go. Not one little bit. AMC Theatres wants to stay in Kips Bay.

	Operating under long term leases, there was a time that the monies headed each month to the theatre’s landlord had risen to become so high that the theatre’s long-term viability was uncertain. But, we were fortunate to have been successful in addressing those concerns in recent years. Today this theatre (one which has been in continuous operation for more than 25 years) has a bright future — if we would be allowed to keep it.
	

	Indeed, every day, thousands of guests watch a movie at AMC Kips Bay 15. It has become so popular of late that on several days this past summer, AMC Kips Bay 15 was repeatedly among the 10 most attended movie theatres across the entire United States, out of the more than 500 theatres operated by AMC nationally.

	In that light, this is a theatre that should not be even close to a permanent shutting off of its lights.

	Of course, AMC wants this AMC movie theatre to stay in place.

	And remembering how much and how often Americans love watching movies in theatres, a tradition in Manhattan that dates back more than a full century, we have heard from so many of you that you too want us to stay open for your benefit.

	Apparently, NYU Langone Health does not share that view, not ours or not yours.

	Unfortunately, the decision to retain or end AMC’s tenure in Kips Bay is not ours to make. The nearby NYU Langone Health facility wants to expand, seems to be in the process of buying the building in which your (our) theatre now operates, and it wants us gone. In anticipation of such a transfer to NYU Langone, the current building’s owner has terminated our lease.

	We have engaged with NYU Langone, suggesting any number of alternatives — including that it enlarge the current low-rise building to satisfy its desires for a growth of its medical facility but also leaving a theatre in place for you. Or alternatively, we offered that our theatre could get smaller, so that at the very least we could leave something remaining in place to continue to serve you. Sadly, any and all variations that we have proposed have fallen on closed minds.

	We call on NYU Langone Health to open their minds, to think creatively, and come up with a solution that will give the Kips Bay community BOTH of the two things that is wanted most of all: expanded facilities offering the world class medical care that is the hallmark of NYU Langone Health AND a fully functional AMC Theatre on Second Avenue.

	It isn’t true that New Yorkers can be prevented from having your cake and eating it too. Indeed you can. But only if people of goodwill think out of the box a bit. After all, the ubiquitous proverb “where there is a will, there is a way” is one that is believed to have first been published in the year 1640 — that’s three hundred eighty six years back to be precise.
	

	Speaking of people of goodwill, I especially want to express gratitude to Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal and New York State Assembly Member Keith Powers, for their leadership and tireless advocacy on this matter. Reinforcing and speaking for the local community’s clear desire, they have energetically brought attention to the importance of keeping an AMC movie theatre open and operating in Kips Bay.

	In summary, this is a theatre that you in Kips Bay want to continue to be at your beck and call, and one that we at AMC unequivocally also want to be allowed to continue within our theatrical fleet.

	But time is short. Unless NYU Langone Health lets us delight the Kips Bay community beyond then, to comply with our terminated lease, the lights on AMC Kips Bay 15 will forevermore see their final sunset on January 3, a mere two and a half months from now.

	Hopefully, there is an outcome in which a wise workable solution is devised, one that will benefit and please the entire neighborhood. What say you NYU Langone Health?

	Whatever happens, I want you to know how much AMC appreciates your support, your efforts and your voice. We are proud to have been part of the Kips Bay community since 1999, and I sincerely hope that we can continue to be part of it for years to come.

	Sincerely,Adam Aron, Chairman of the Board and Chief Executive Officer AMC Entertainment

title: Quentin Tarantino Surprises Fans With 17 Minutes of ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ at AFI Fest
description: Quentin Tarantino surprised audiences on Friday night at AFI Fest when he shared the first 17 minutes of “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth
body:
Quentin Tarantino surprised audiences on Friday night at AFI Fest when he shared the first 17 minutes of “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”

	Tarantino made a special appearance at the TCL Chinese Theatre in Hollywood, following a screening of “Once Upon a Time … In Hollywood.” Following the Q&A moderated by Rotten Tomatoes’ Jacqueline Coley, the filmmaker said, “Well, I could talk a little bit about ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ or I could show you the first 17 minutes.”
	

	Directed by David Fincher, who was also in attendance, the film sees the return of Cliff Booth played by Brad Pitt. The film picks up in 1977 from the original film’s 1969 timeline. The logline reads: “Los Angeles no longer needs a hippie-slaying stuntman the way it did. But Hollywood will always have problems, problems that can only be solved by someone with Cliff’s unique (occasionally extralegal) abilities. When he’s not earning his keep bartending or as a projectionist, Cliff Booth is a fixer — solving situations for Hollywood’s great and, sometimes, not so good.”


	He’s curious when he gets a call from talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), on behalf of her client, TV megastar Charlie Peters (Scott Caan) — a man known for doing his own stunts. And he’s further entertained and intrigued when he meets other characters in Charlie’s world, from his knowing wife Toni (Carla Gugino) to pro football champion turned screen star Roderick “Hot Rod” Harrison (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II). Then there are the Verdusco brothers (Matt Groove and JB Tadena), mysterious gangsters causing mayhem across the city. What was once a fairytale is now a crime story — a cocktail of violence, ambition and desire that could only happen in LA.
	

	Tarantino, who wrote the screenplay, shared his decision to revisit Cliff Booth. He said, “I tend to not remember good reviews of mine in quotes; I remember the bad reviews in quotes, but I don’t really remember good reviews of mine in quotes. But one quote that I do remember somebody writing about ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ was, ‘This seems like the first world Quentin Tarantino has ever created that he would like to live in’ and there is that aspect; I loved the Cliff Booth character,” Tarantino said. “I loved the way that Brad played him, and there was this aspect of him as sort of like a paperback hero. I could see like a series of paperbacks with Cliff Booth getting involved with this adventure or that adventure or something like that.”

	While further plot details can’t be spoiled, the opening sequence has Tarantino’s distinguished style of writing and visually, the Hollywood of 1977 is, in true Fincher style, gritty and dark. 

	The Netflix film also stars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and Peter Weller and is set to premiere in Imax theaters on Nov. 25, before hitting the streamer Dec. 23.

	The evening kicked off with Tarantino introducing the film and shared that had not seen the film at that theater. 

	In the Q&A, Tarantino shared how he had spoken with Burt Reynolds about playing the George Spahn character. Tarantino recalled, “He said yes and we became friendly, but he passed away before we could make the film. But we did get to rehearse with him and do the script reading with him, so actually, the last performance Burt Reynolds ever gave was as George Spahn in the script reading.”

	The character would be played by Bruce Dern.

	He also talked about his upcoming play “The Popinjay Cavalier,” which stars Sacha Baron Cohen and is set to premiere in London’s West End next year. “I’m not going to talk a whole lot about that, but our previews are in February. In November we’ll start rehearsals.” He went on to say, “I’m just a writer and that’s just kind of what I do. I’m always writing.”

title: El Gouna Takeaways: ‘Safe Exit’ Wins Top Prize, Arab TV Seeks New Talent and Egyptian Filmmakers Push Boundaries
description: Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival wrapped its ninth edition Friday after nine days of screenings, industry activity and a closing night that spread it
body:
Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival wrapped its ninth edition Friday after nine days of screenings, industry activity and a closing night that spread its top prizes across the Middle East and beyond.

	Mohammed Hammad’s “Safe Exit,” a psychological drama about a young Coptic security guard in Cairo confronting trauma rooted in religious violence, won the Golden Star for best narrative feature. Ahmed Hassouna’s “Citizen Osama,” following a Gaza photojournalist balancing his work with family life amid war, took both the Golden Star for documentary and best Arab documentary. Anders Davidsen’s “Stolen Memories,” in which the discovery of childhood photographs leads an 18-year-old to question his past, won the Golden Star for short film. Rakan Mayasi’s Bekaa Valley-set “Yesterday the Eye Didn’t Sleep” was named best Arab narrative, while Marie Rose Ousta’s “One Day Born,” about an 11-year-old boy living under the constant threat of warplanes in Lebanon, took best Arab short.
	

	Jordan’s Rakeen Saad won best actress for Zaid Abu Hamdan’s “Boomah,” while Jovan Ginić took best actor for Miroslav Terzić’s “3 Weeks After.”


	Here are five takeaways from this year’s festival.

	CineGouna, the Industry Platform, Is Becoming the Main Event

	“We want the industry to be our hero,” El Gouna co-founder and executive director Amr Mansi told Variety ahead of this year’s festival.

	The ninth edition made good on that ambition. More than 320 projects applied to CineGouna Funding, with 19 selected projects ultimately receiving more than $350,000 across 40 awards, while participants held more than 140 one-on-one meetings with companies, institutions and international festivals.
	

	The activity extended beyond financing. CineGouna now encompasses Funding; Forum, a program of panels, masterclasses and industry discussions; Market, which connects filmmakers with companies and institutions; and Emerge, its initiative for young and emerging talent. This year also brought Egyptian Voices, a development program for Egyptian filmmakers, and an inaugural Series lab for Arab television projects into the fold. CineGouna is becoming as central to El Gouna’s identity as the films it screens.

	Arab TV Is Searching for a Development Pipeline

	CineGouna’s expansion into television also highlighted a wider problem confronting Arab television: there’s an abundance of talent, but opportunities to develop and sell new shows are sorely lacking.

	Veteran Egyptian screenwriter and producer Mariam Naoum, who spearheaded the six-week CineGouna Series development lab, told Variety there are “great, great talents” in the region, but only “three or four platforms,” leaving creators competing for limited outlets.

	Producer and screenwriter Haitham Dabbour similarly noted that fewer platforms make buyers more cautious, while director Mariam Abou Ouf warned that the business is “approaching a deadlock.” The six projects selected for the inaugural lab came to El Gouna to pitch their series and meet potential industry partners, with the aim of moving the projects closer to production.

	Displaced Filmmakers Need More Than a Platform

	War and displacement continue to shape filmmaking across the Arab world, affecting not only the stories reaching screens but the filmmakers trying to build careers.

	The first Safe Harbour MENA, launched with the International Film Festival Rotterdam and the International Emerging Film Talent Association, brought four filmmakers displaced within the region into a program of training, project development and industry networking.

	The initiative reframed support less as simply offering filmmakers a platform to tell stories about displacement than giving them the professional connections needed to continue working. “Citizen Osama’s” double win offered a potent reminder of the circumstances confronting filmmakers in the region: director Ahmed Hassouna remains in Gaza.

	Egyptian Filmmakers Are Pushing for More Creative Freedom
	

	“Safe Exit’s” top prize landed amid a broader conversation at El Gouna about an Egyptian industry in transition.

	Producer Mohammad Mashish pointed to a younger generation with “more freedom than before” and audiences increasingly exposed to international cinema, but argued that the industry needs more time for development and screenwriting.

	Producer-distributor Ziad Srouji put the challenge more succinctly: “Specificity travels, generic does not.” Muhammad Mustapha, whose documentary “Big Boys Don’t Cry” premiered at El Gouna, similarly argued for models that lower financial risk while allowing filmmakers to take greater artistic risks.

	The tension is increasingly clear: Egyptian filmmakers are looking outward while asking for enough room to make work rooted firmly at home.

	El Gouna Looks Beyond El Gouna

	One of the festival’s most locally significant launches will take place largely after its guests have gone home.

	Cinema on Wheels is taking three shorts from this year’s lineup on a free screening tour through Hurghada, Minya, Qena, Luxor and Aswan before concluding in Cairo, accompanied by discussions with audiences.

	“We’re always exploring ways to increase the reach of El Gouna Film Festival beyond just its duration and the town of El Gouna,” artistic director Andrew Mohsen explained.

	For a festival built in an affluent Red Sea resort, the effort to bring its programming to audiences elsewhere in Egypt significantly expands its reach. As Mansi put it: “Cinema on Wheels is our way of connecting El Gouna to the rest of the country.”

title: ‘Love Language’ Review: Chloë Grace Moretz Sells Words of Affirmation in an Old-School Romcom With Gen-Z Trappings
description: Much has been written on the new dating politics practiced by Gen-Z — more progressive socially, more conservative sexually, if you believe the hot
body:
Much has been written on the new dating politics practiced by Gen-Z — more progressive socially, more conservative sexually, if you believe the hot takes, which you probably shouldn’t. Either way, that sensibility has yet to trickle down to mainstream portrayals of Zoomer romance on screen, which remain largely beholden to templates established by previous generations. “Love Language” is the latest in a line of youthful romantic comedies in nostalgic thrall to ’90s tropes of the genre, from klutzy meet-cutes to gay best friends to climactic airport interventions, and if it modestly updates proceedings with queer marriage and cocaine jokes, it still suggests that our species’ mating rituals have largely held fast. That Joey Power‘s palatable, attractively assembled film will likely be a comfort watch for many under-30s should in turn be a comfort to their elders. 
	

	Like many latter-day romcoms, “Love Language” is cozily, even sentimentally romantic, while neglecting the comic half of the equation — despite a premise with ample potential for wit. Chloë Grace Moretz stars as Louisa, an allegedly gifted but perennially blocked writer who chances into an unexpectedly lucrative side hustle penning other people’s wedding vows, all while struggling to articulate her own messy romantic feelings for two different men. It’s a solid setup, but Power (who last directed the 2018 romance “After Everything,” starring Jeremy Allen White and Maika Monroe) isn’t the best with words himself: The film coasts off the combined charms of its ensemble and location, with Chicago shot in warm, perma-autumnal tones, and thus goes down quite easily. It would be nice, though, if it was funny too.
	

	Well, you can’t have everything — as a jaded Louisa, recently burned by a broken-off engagement, is wont to think. Her broken heart makes her something of a killjoy at the bachelorette party of her best friend Tilda (Billie Lourd), but does present an upside for the bride-to-be: When Tilda asks Louisa to help with her wedding vows, Louisa merely repurposes those she had written for her own aborted nuptials. Her style may be a bit “Hallmark × Rupi Kaur” but the vows go down a treat, and when word gets out at the wedding that Louisa ghostwrote them, total strangers approach her to request their own dewy-eyed dedications. It’s a productive wedding all round: She also meets Tilda’s sexy cousin Dash (a terrific Anthony Ramos), and though she’s a little thrown by his straight-talking manner, there’s clearly a spark between them.

	She’s quickly distracted, however, when she’s commissioned by wealthy importer Olivia (Isabel May) to write her vows for her upcoming wedding to dreamboat public defender Warren (Manny Jacinto) — who, it turns out, is Louisa’s old college crush. Taking the job while keeping that fact from Olivia, she finds old feelings rekindled as she spends more time with the couple; at the same time, she casually dates Dash, but discourages his more serious advances. And as Olivia and Warren’s big day draws nearer, she finds herself unable to write a word.

	It’s a romantic quadrangle in which the two most storied individuals are also the least interesting. Moretz capably juggles Louisa’s neuroses and delusions, not shying from the character’s tendency toward selfishness and self-pity, but it’s May’s Olivia, cannily played as both a princess and an underestimated observer, whom we want to know better. And while we’re treated to multiple scenes of Louisa and Warren hanging out and fondly reflecting on old times, he’s not half as charismatic or ultimately soul-baring as Dash is — which makes her romantic dilemma feel overly protracted and low-stakes, evading the emotional complexities of an evenly weighted choice. (The premise is plainly a nod to the likewise Chicago-set genre standard “My Best Friend’s Wedding,” though the beauty of that film is that it presented Julia Roberts’ protagonist with altogether less enviable options: homewrecking or continued singledom.)
	

	Perhaps the script is unduly tilted by Ramos’ drawling, sincerely beguiling delivery. Handed a fairly two-dimensional character concept — fuckboi with a nesting impulse — he crafts a personality that feels more embedded in the real world than everyone else here. Moretz’s performance, too, is livelier and more limber in his presence; away from him, Louisa feels a bit floatily conceived. Her day job (as a WFH copywriter), friendships (including with Lukas Gage’s gay lothario turned broody plot device) and even her apartment want for detail and texture, as “Love Language” largely colors its story with allusions to other movies and pop ephemera. It’s a pleasant, undemanding watch in large part because it’s all so very recognizable, but one wonders when a more generationally defining romcom will come along.

title: Morelia Film Festival Prizes: ‘Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building,’ an ‘Expression of Pure, Unbound Beauty,’ Wins Top ‘Ojo’ Award
description: Bruno Santamaría Razo’s fiction debut “Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building”(“Seis meses en el edificio rosa con azul”) has clinched the top Ojo
body:
Bruno Santamaría Razo’s fiction debut “Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building”(“Seis meses en el edificio rosa con azul”) has clinched the top Ojo award at the 24th Morelia Film Festival (FICM), which wraps Oct. 25.

	Hailed by Variety as a “lush, poetic film rooted in memories,” it became the first Mexican feature to compete at Cannes’ Critics Week in 20 years.

	Morelia’s international jury, led by J.A. Bayona (“Society of the Snow”), praised the coming-of-age film for “courageously exploring the past, embracing pain and transforming it …into an expression of pure, unbound beauty.”
	

	Drawing on the filmmaker’s own experiences, the drama traces back to a defining moment in his childhood: the year he turned eleven and when his father was diagnosed with HIV.

	“Six Months…” also nabbed the Audience Award for fiction films, a strong indication of its box office potential.

	Alejandro Ramírez, Cinépolis CEO and FICM president, described the festival’s 24th edition as a particularly Mexican celebration as it welcomed some of Mexico’s finest filmmakers and actors, including Guillermo del Toro, Alfonso Cuarón, Carlos Reygadas, Jonás Cuarón, Diego Luna, Gael García Bernal, Demián Bichir, Diego Boneta and Luis Gerardo Méndez.

	With James Gray in town to present his crime drama “Paper Tiger” and J.A. Bayona serving as jury president, the festival has enjoyed a standout edition, he noted. Bayona also presented “Beyond Society,” a three-part documentary about the making of “Society of the Snow.”

	“I think the films this year represent the wide diversity of Mexican cinematic imagination,” festival director Daniel Michel observed.
	

	“There are many different and fascinating stories covering the breadth of experiences in our country which, we hope, will find a home in cinemas, as well as a large spectatorship. We’re also very proud to represent very different regions; Mexico is not a country one can easily summarize, but, rather, a vast territory with many differences which, I believe, our official selection has tried to gather in a single place.”

	Meanwhile, Joaquin del Paso’s “The Garden We Dreamed,” which turns on a Haitian family traveling north in search of a better future, snagged two awards: a Special Mention and Best Cinematography for its DP, Gökhan Tiryaki.

	“Sad Girlz,” a buzz film at the fest, was recognized as the best fiction debut with the Casa Wabis-Escine award, lauded by the jury for its “genuine performances” and “impeccable exploration of a young modern teen’s life, with all its complexities and contradictions.”

	The rest of the awards were quite evenly distributed. Santiago Maza, whose “Black Shine” competed among the short films, won the ECAM award, a scholarship for a Master’s degree in distribution from the prestigious Madrid Film School (ECAM).

	Nicolas Pereda snapped up the Best Director award with his absurdist comedy “Everything Else Is Noise,” which also snagged his lead Teresa Sanchez (“Flies”) a Best Actress Ojo prize for her performance as Tere, a cello musician-composer in whose apartment her colleague Rosa arranges her first television interview.

	Sam Louwyck won the Best Actor prize for his portrayal of a gay hairdresser in Nathalia Acevedo’s “Beauty Salon,” where his salon serves as a refuge for marginalized people.

	Noted Michel: “We’re also very pleased to have had directors from very different backgrounds and identities who have brought their perspectives and very singular ideas on filmmaking to our festival.”

	Next year, the festival will be moving its dates back to the last week before the Day of the Dead. FICM is already gearing up for its 25th anniversary, promising a landmark edition with major guests, bold retrospectives and a stellar lineup.

	Among the highlights of the 10-day festival:

	“Naza”

	Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary “Naza” – which means collateral damage – played to a packed Teatro Matamoros after which it unsurprisingly won an audience award. Unlike its reception at the 83rd Venice Film Festival, where it won the Special Jury Prize and received a record-breaking standing ovation, it was met with stunned silence as the credits rolled.
	

	Presenting the documentary beforehand was festival VP Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas Batel who underscored the importance of the screening to help audiences understand such a complex conflict. He noted that the Israeli filmmakers have been unable to return to their country after being accused of treason, adding that such accusations by a “criminal government” are a source of pride for those working toward peaceful solutions.

	He reaffirmed the festival’s commitment to peace, dialogue and ending violence worldwide, calling for an end to the ongoing genocide against the Palestinian people.

	Film critic Alonso Díaz de la Vega, also spoke, describing Naza as a “deeply moving” film that exposes not only the genocide in Gaza but also the global implications of military technology, artificial intelligence and surveillance.

	“The most important thing this screening can inspire is not silence, but the words ‘Free Palestine,’” Díaz de la Vega concluded. The film opens in select theaters in Mexico on Oct. 22.

	Guillermo del Toro Rules

	At the festival to present the 3D re-release of his much-lauded “Pan’s Labyrinth,” the anti-authoritarian theme of his Oscar-winning fable hit home even harder this time, given the rise of right-wing governments across the region and the world at large.

	Speaking to hordes of mostly young fans at his Masterclass and later at a press conference and multiple one-on-one interviews, the indefatigable filmmaker reflected on the current state of affairs in the world.

	He grew emotional at the presser when he said: “The state of our species and society today goes beyond anything we could have imagined back then. But I recognize the same sadness and despair. It pains me deeply to see one, two, or three generations fail the next. We’re handing down a world in ruins, morally, socially and spiritually fractured, with the very fabric that once allowed us to tell fables and parables falling apart.”

	French-Mexican Alliance 

	As part of the partnership established in 2003 between FICM and Cannes Critics’ Week, this year’s edition presented a selection of eight films and one short that screened at the sidebar last May. Ava Cahen, artistic director of the Cannes Film Festival’s parallel section, led the screenings, which included such titles as Aina Clotet’s “Viva,” Alexander Murphy’s “Tin Castle” and Zou Jing’s “A Girl Unknown.”
	

	Toasting Mexico and France’s 200 years of diplomatic relations this year, French ambassador to Mexico Delphine Borione awarded Alfonso Cuarón the insignia of Officer of the Order of Arts and Letters during the fest to honor his “extraordinary contribution to contemporary cinema, singular vision, artistic reinvention and role in bringing Mexican culture to global audiences.”

	Calling Cuarón “one of the greatest filmmakers of our time,” she praised his universal vision and the cultural ties his work has forged between Mexico and France. “To speak to the world, one must never stop being oneself,” she said, reflecting on his films, from “Y Tu Mamá También” to “Roma.”

	Reflecting on France’s deep influence on his filmmaking, Cuarón described cinema as “not a narrative art, but a musical art” – a rhythmic, organic creation with its own heartbeat and a direct image of time.

	He closed by addressing France’s current political turmoil, expressing hope that young people’s calls for change would be heard rather than co-opted by opportunism. Quoting French writer Pascal Quignard, he concluded: “I do not believe art can ever be negative. It ignores negation because it ignores time.”

description:
Six Flags Over Georgia
                          Goliath Roller Coaster To Reopen With Seat Belts
body:
Six Flags Over Georgia
                          Goliath Roller Coaster To Reopen With Seat Belts
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 24, 2026
                            11:14 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Six Flags Over Georgia's Goliath roller coaster is set to be reopened with new safety features once the ride has been retrofitted ... after a man was violently thrown to his death earlier this month.
      
    
            The theme park announced seat belts would be added to the ride ... as well as other rides with similar restraints ... CEO John Reilly revealed in a statement Friday.
      
    
            Reilly added ... "Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia remains closed pending necessary safety reviews and clearances. Eight additional rides at five other parks are temporarily closed out of an abundance of caution. Our parks remain open, including throughout Halloween weekend, with more than 220 roller coasters operating across our parks."
      

            We reported earlier ... Hassan Kariem died after he became unrestrained during the ride, flew off the coaster and struck the tracks multiple times.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            In the wake of his death ... parks across the country temporarily halted operations on several high-speed coasters with similar lap bar restraints.
      
    
            Kariem's family told us that he was laid to rest earlier this week.
      
    
            The educator was only 42.
      
    
            RIP

            Anika Rashaun -- who starred on hit reality shows like "The Challenge" and "The Real World" -- has died from breast cancer ... her friends have revealed.
      
    
            The TV star-turned-dating coach died on Oct. 1 after being diagnosed with cancer last summer.
      
    
            Cyndi Rich wrote on Facebook ... "Anika shined so bright. Being close to that light as one of her closest friends was a true blessing. She is a vibrant soul. I’ll love her and treasure the 16 years of memories forever."
      

            Another friend Tiara Ramos wrote on Substack ... "Anika Rashaun Walker Rehn was part of my life longer than she wasn’t. She was my mirror: the good, the bad, the ugly, the really ugly. She wasn’t just my friend. She was my other half. If you knew me, you knew her."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Tiara also wrote that despite the fact her mother had breast cancer years earlier ... "she was never identified as high-risk or told by her doctors to prioritize mammograms."
      
    
            She added ... "That was one of the many failures she experienced within the medical system during her time battling cancer."
      
    
            Anika -- who previously appeared on "The Real World" 2016-2017 "Bad Blood" season and on "The Challenge: Invasion of the Champions" in 2017 -- was 34.
